title: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
content:
Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.
Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.
It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.
Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.
So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?
Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.
It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.
"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.
But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.
Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point".
"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.
When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs.
Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.
She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.
On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.
Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.
Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.
But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue , telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.
Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.
Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.

title: What's really going on with the lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?
content:
If she's ever feeling bloated, Abbey Alexandra has a go-to routine, using body oil and a wooden roller to perform stomach massages.
The 31-year-old from Birmingham shares before-and-after videos on TikTok, saying she feels the process leaves her depuffed and defined: "You definitely feel a lot better after, they are relaxing."
The technique is a form of lymphatic drainage massage, adapted from a medical treatment and shared as a beauty trend. Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them."
Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". But what's actually happening to their bodies?
Many videos on social media promoting lymphatic massage show a woman either standing sideways, facing the front or perhaps lying down with her stomach showing a slight - and very normal - curve outwards.
Then begins the methodical massage in circular motions seemingly draining fluid away. By the end, her stomach appears flatter - if a little red.
But social media body trends should always be viewed with scepticism, says Dr Ella Guest, senior research fellow and health psychologist at the Centre for Appearance Research based at the University of the West of England.
"These images might be altered using photo-editing tools or filters, people standing in particular poses, use of lighting, lots could even be AI-generated," she says.
"I think stopping to reflect on what you see and questioning whether it looks realistic, or if it's very aligned with beauty standards, can be useful. Remember, if something looks too good to be true, it probably is."
The lymphatic system is a network of channels and glands throughout the body that helps fight infection and remove excess fluid, according to the NHS.
Dr Xand van Tulleken tells Morning Live that the lymphatic system helps remove excess fluid from tissues and supports the immune system.
"When it is not working properly, it can contribute to swelling, which can be a condition called lymphoedema."
This commonly affects people who have cancers that involve the lymph system or who've had treatment involving the lymph nodes.
It causes swelling in any part of the body, but usually develops in the arms or legs.
"In simple terms, the lymphatic system helps keep your body's fluid levels balanced, cleans up waste, and supports your defences against illness," says van Tulleken.
Dr Xand says manual lymphatic drainage is one of a range of treatments used by medical professionals "if your lymphatic system isn't working as it should".
He describes it as using "light pressure" and "strategic massage techniques" to "clear" your lymphatic system.
"They'll coax excess lymph fluid from your swollen tissues toward your lymph nodes, where the lymph can reabsorb," he says - adding lymph nodes are found in the armpits, neck and groin.
He adds that these massages can be a "safe way" to relieve symptoms for conditions like lymphoedema but are not suitable for some people with pre-existing medical conditions.
He stresses: "No one should get their health advice from Instagram - far safer to use the NHS website, or consult your GP."

title: New WHO estimates show changing global health landscape
content:
The global health landscape continues to evolve and people are living longer. Following the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, global life expectancy has returned to close to pre-pandemic levels. At the same time, noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) account for an increasing share of deaths, with conditions such as diabetes, dementia, mental health conditions and drug use disorders contributing to a growing and changing burden of disease.
WHO’s latest Global Health Estimates , released today, provide a picture of how health has changed across countries and regions between 2000 and 2023, including trends in life expectancy, causes of death and disease burden.
Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, close to the 73.4 years recorded in 2019. Healthy life expectancy has recovered more slowly, reaching 62.8 years in 2023, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level.
At the same time, the long-term shift towards NCDs continues. NCDs accounted for 74% of deaths globally in 2023, compared with 58% in 2000. Eight of the world’s ten leading causes of death were NCDs in 2023.
This shift is increasingly visible across all income levels. In 2023, for the first time, communicable diseases accounted for less than half of all deaths in low-income countries, marking another step in the global epidemiological transition.
“Living longer is one of the great achievements of public health,” said Dr Alain Labrique, Director of WHO’s Department of Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI. “The next challenge is to ensure that those additional years are lived in good health, while health systems are equipped to respond to the changing needs of populations.”
Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of death and disease burden worldwide. In 2023, ischaemic heart disease alone caused approximately 9.5 million deaths and 210 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), measured in years of healthy life lost.
There has been substantial progress in reducing the burden of ischaemic heart disease since 2000 in many parts of the world. However, increases in risk at an individual level were recorded in the WHO Western Pacific and South-East Asia Regions, highlighting persistent inequalities in cardiovascular health between populations.
Other chronic conditions are also becoming increasingly prominent. The risk of dying from diabetes has risen substantially since 2000, particularly in South-East Asia. Alzheimer disease and other dementias have also risen sharply, for example dementia became the fifth leading cause of death globally in 2023, compared with 19th in 2000. Global deaths from dementia tripled over this period.
Mental health conditions are another important part of the changing global health picture. Between 2019 and 2023, the global age-standardized DALY rate increased by approximately 20% for depressive disorders and nearly 45% for anxiety disorders. Together, these conditions accounted for an estimated 110 million years of healthy life loss through premature death and disability in 2023.
Drug use disorders showed similar trends across regions. Between 2000 and 2023, the WHO Region of the Americas recorded the largest increases in risk of mortality and healthy life loss while the Western Pacific saw substantial declines.
Taken together, the estimates show a global health landscape that is both recovering from the pandemic and continuing to evolve.
“The value of these estimates is not only in the numbers themselves,” said Dr Labrique. “By showing how causes of death and disease burden are changing over time and across populations, they give countries evidence to help shape health policies and priorities. They also help WHO support countries in building resilient, essential digital and data infrastructure while strengthening national and subnational capacity to analyse health data and generate timely, actionable insights. These capabilities are critical to better enable targeted, effective interventions and ultimately further improving health and well-being for all.”
The Global Health Estimates provide estimates of causes of death and disability across countries and regions and over time. They enable policy-makers and health partners to track changes in population health, identify emerging trends and better understand where further action is needed.

As soon as my son pressed play, the video made me wince. A few years ago, he’d discretely recorded me from the backseat as I was driving, talking to my other son in the passenger seat. We were returning from one of their junior tennis matches and I was questioning what I had perceived to be a lack of effort. As I watched it back, I told myself that it could have been worse; I wasn’t angry but seeing it many years later made me wish I could take it all back. Earlier this summer, I thought about those days again when Melanie Bedard’s 2023 interview with the Toronto Star about “the drive home” resurfaced. Her son Connor was just named captain of the Chicago Blackhawks, and is considered one of the best professional hockey players of his generation. “Connor would say some of his teammates would be crying because they didn’t want to go on the car rides with their dad, with their parents,” she said of his early days in the game. “And I thought, all these people in this machine, you are losing sight of the most important thing, your relation. “Because even if they are the next (NHL hockey legend Sidney) Crosby, they’ll probably be done in their 30s and you’ve damaged that relationship that you could have had for the rest of your life,” she said. The “drive home” is a recognized experience, almost a rite of passage that many young athletes will have to endure immediately after a disappointing practice or game, trapped inside a vehicle when the emotions are most raw. It’s one of the reasons that many children fall out of love with sports: 70% of youth athletes drop out of organized sports by the age of 13, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. When I pitched the idea of this story to my editor, his reaction was visceral “I remember those rides home with my dad,” he said, rolling his eyes. Buried in my own subconscious is the memory of my father telling me of his embarrassment when I’d trailed in last place in a 400-meter race at my English middle school. Every season, millions of young athletes are being driven home by parents navigating what to say, if anything, and how to say it. A typical scene was created for a 2016 “True Sport” public service film in Canada: “So, not your best practice,” begins the father’s disappointed monologue as he turns the key in the ignition. “Was something wrong? Because you seem distracted. Can we agree on that?” The camera slowly pans around the car to reveal a young boy sitting diagonally behind him, in silence. “It seemed like you wanted to hang out with your friends more than practice. Maybe we can skip your next game. That way, I don’t have to rush home from work to sit on a freezing cold bench for two hours to watch you and your buddies jerk around.” The put-downs keep on coming, each one cutting deeper than the last, “Wasting your time’s one thing, wasting my time and your coach’s time, that’s selfish. Maybe that’s who you are.” “The number one reason why kids leave sport is because it’s not fun anymore,” said Karri Dawson, True Sport Foundation’s former executive director. She told CNN that the campaign was designed to speak to the average, well-intentioned parents who may not be aware of the power of their words. In some cases, it was profoundly successful, Dawson said. “They were like, ‘Oh my word!’ People reaching out to me saying, ‘I had no idea that the things I was saying and doing may be having such a negative impact on my child’s enjoyment.’” What plays out in those car rides home has actually been studied by Jeemin Kim, assistant professor of kinesiology at Michigan State University, who worked with the late Katherine Tamminen to understand those conversations. Their findings were published in January 2022. While admitting to a probable sampling bias, because overbearing parents are unlikely to allow GoPro cameras to record their post-game interactions, Kim said that he was generally encouraged by the 28 parent-child pairings and 30 hours of footage he observed. “There’s this narrative of youth sport, parents are crazy, they’re always screaming at their kids, but that just wasn’t the case,” Kim told CNN. The study revealed that 59% of the recording was silence. “When emotions are running high, it’s not a bad thing to sit there and then let the emotions cool down,” he added. The study revealed that sport was only discussed 13% of the time and that parents provided more praise about their child’s performance than the athlete did themselves. “In several instances, parents interjected before athletes could respond to their parents’ comments,” Kim said. Researchers also interviewed the parents and their athlete children. “I remember one kid saying something along the lines of, ‘I love playing the sport, but you don’t play to have these conversations,’” he added. “If that’s the memory they’re going to have associated with youth sport, they’re not going to remember it as good.” Few of us have the wherewithal to be as disciplined as Richard Williams, who famously banned tennis talk with his daughters Venus and Serena on the way home. I remember reading that the father of two of the most famous tennis stars on the planet wanted to preserve the innocence of their youth for as long as possible. It was an edict that applied whether they had won or lost – there would be no recriminations, but he wouldn’t entertain any gloating either. Several US-based organizations have highlighted the ride home as a critical element of a child’s sports enjoyment, but even some of the most vocal advocates admit that it’s not always easy. Former professional soccer player John O’Sullivan, who founded the Changing the Game Project, once admitted that he couldn’t help himself when his son TJ didn’t want to play in the first game for the team that he was coaching. “On the car ride home, I felt the need to address this issue,” he wrote on his website, explaining that his wife karate-chopped him across the chest as soon as he addressed their five-year-old in the back seat. “Really, didn’t you just write a whole book about this?” she shot back with a stern look. It’s an anecdote that many parents will relate to – O’Sullivan was worried that his son would miss out on a game that he had loved all his life. He advises parents now to just to say five words when everyone is back in the car: “I love watching you play.” Regardless of their age, most athletes know when they have messed up. They don’t need to be told. They may also need time to process their own emotions about the game, and a parent’s lecture on the way home may kick off before they’ve fully come to terms with what just happened. The author of several books about peak performance, and a coach of his children’s youth teams, Brad Stulberg understands how consequential these moments can be. “The worst thing you can do is analyze the game,” he told CNN. “And even if they played great, you’re sending a message to the kid, like, ‘Well if I didn’t play great, are you not going to be excited to be with me?’ “I think the kids just want to be kids, and if they want to talk about what happened, they’ll tell you. But generally, my experience is they don’t.” Looking back on those drives with my twins, who are both now in college, our best rides home were the ones that never focused on tennis. On one occasion, as one of my sons was starting to get into music, he’d play a track and ask me to guess how long was left on the song. The first time he asked, I nailed it. Somehow, I knew that there were exactly 27 seconds left on “Wonderwall” by Oasis. His eyes lit up as if I’d just performed some kind of sorcery. It was beginners’ luck, and I never did it again. But it was a magical moment. My boys dropped tennis after high school and are now in a college band together. When they were starting out as budding musicians, the drives home from practice or those early “School of Rock”-style performances were always joyful. There was never any chatter about off-tempo rhythms or missed notes. That’s how I should have done it for sport, too. Nobody wants to be criticized for something that is supposed to be fun, and if you ruin all the fun, don’t be surprised if they don’t want to do it for much longer. Just love watching them play, and talk about anything else.
